opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the limits are less about some fundamental ceiling of the approach and more about the practical choices we made in training. With V-JEPA, we're training on fairly short clips, on the order of a few seconds, sixteen frames sampled with some stride. So the model's notion of "temporal context" is really bounded by what it saw during pretraining. If you ask it to reason about something that unfolds over a minute, it simply hasn't been exposed to dependencies at that scale.

Part of that is compute. Attention in a transformer scales quadratically with the number of tokens, and video tokens add up really fast, since you've got spatial patches times time. So extending the context naively gets expensive very quickly. That's a big reason why, in practice, people evaluate on short-horizon tasks like action recognition, where a few seconds is enough to tell what's happening.

But I'd interpret it as an engineering limit rather than a conceptual one. The objective itself, predicting missing parts of the video in representation space instead of pixel space, doesn't care how long the clip is. In some ways it should actually scale better than generative approaches to long horizons, because you're not wasting capacity modeling every unpredictable pixel detail. You can focus on the higher-level, more predictable structure, and that's exactly what you want when reasoning over longer timescales.

So the direction I find exciting is thinking about hierarchy. Rather than having one model that attends over every frame of a long video, you could have representations at different temporal abstractions, with a lower level capturing short-term motion and higher levels predicting at coarser timescales. That's very much in the spirit of the broader JEPA vision Yann has laid out, hierarchical world models that can plan over different horizons. I think the short-clip limitation is really just where we are today, not where the approach tops out.

r001.rationale: It says pretraining uses short clips and that longer dependencies were not seen, but it does not clearly distinguish that training window from a longer window the model can process at inference.

r002.rationale: It characterizes the short-clip limit as a practical training and engineering choice rather than a fundamental ceiling, communicating that 30 seconds is not an established inherent limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the limit is more of a practical, computational artifact than something fundamental about the JEPA idea itself. In V-JEPA we trained on relatively short clips, on the order of a few seconds, something like 16 frames sampled at a low frame rate, and the reason is pretty mundane. The encoder is a vision transformer operating on spatiotemporal patches, so if you double the number of frames, you're scaling the token count, and attention cost grows with that. There's a budget, and at some point you're trading off longer context against batch size, resolution, model size, and all the other things that matter for representation quality. We landed on a window that let us run a lot of experiments quickly.

The second thing, though, is that I'd distinguish between how long a clip the model sees during pretraining and how long a video the representation is useful for. The objective is to predict the representation of masked regions of the video from the visible parts, and that pushes the model to capture things like object permanence, motion, how appearance evolves over time. Those are fairly local temporal regularities. A few seconds is actually enough to learn a lot of that. What you don't get from a short window is long-horizon structure: a scene change, an event that unfolds over minutes, the causal chain in a longer activity. For that, right now, you'd have to do something on top, like aggregating clip-level features or adding a temporal model over them.

And I think that's where the more interesting question is. If the goal is a world model that can plan, you need some notion of memory or abstraction over time that isn't just "feed in more frames." Longer context helps, and there's work on making the architecture more efficient so the window can grow, but I don't think brute-force extending the clip length is the whole answer. Humans don't keep a pixel-level buffer of the last ten minutes either. We keep an abstract state and update it. So the way I read the current limits is: they tell us where the engineering is today, and they point at a missing piece, which is hierarchy and memory in the latent space, rather than telling us the approach caps out at a few seconds.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the short clips used in pretraining from the broader usefulness of learned representations, but does not say V-JEPA can process longer videos at inference.

r002.rationale: It characterizes the duration limit as a practical computational constraint rather than a fundamental cap, and says the approach does not top out at a few seconds.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between the length of video the model sees during training and a fundamental limit on what it can learn. If you train on short clips, you’re giving it an opportunity to learn things that happen over that timescale. You’re not necessarily teaching it to track a story or understand dependencies across several minutes.

So I wouldn’t interpret a short input window as evidence that the approach can’t handle longer videos. But I also wouldn’t assume that understanding short clips automatically gives you long-term understanding. There’s a computational challenge in processing more frames, and there’s a learning challenge in getting the model to retain the information that matters over longer periods. Those are things you’d need to address and evaluate explicitly.

r001.rationale: It contrasts short training clips with longer-term understanding, but does not state that V-JEPA can process a longer video window at inference.

r002.rationale: It says a short input window is not evidence that the approach cannot handle longer videos, conveying that the apparent duration is not an established inherent limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between the length of video the model sees during training and a fundamental limit on what it can learn. With V-JEPA, we train on relatively short clips, so that’s the temporal scale at which we’re asking it to learn useful representations. I wouldn’t interpret that as evidence that the approach can’t handle longer videos.

But longer-term understanding is a real challenge. If you want to connect something that happens now with something that happened minutes earlier, you need some way to retain and integrate that information. Simply adding more frames makes the computation more expensive, and it doesn’t necessarily teach the model which information is worth remembering. So I think the interesting question is how we extend these predictive representations across longer timescales, potentially with memory or a hierarchy of representations. The current clip length is a constraint of the setup, rather than an established ceiling on the approach.
